title: Hash, encrypt, or throw away
summary: Choose the right cryptographic tool for passwords and reset tokens, and review a token flow that chose wrong.

scenario.briefing: The campus portal added password reset. A review found tokens generated with Math.random, stored exactly as sent, and never expiring. Before fixing it, decide which cryptographic tool belongs to each secret.

objectives.description: Match passwords and tokens to the right cryptographic operation.
Identify weak token generation, storage, and expiry.
Explain password, token, and transport protections.

hints: Passwords need a slow, salted, one-way function.
Reset tokens need unpredictable randomness and hashed storage.
Encryption is reversible; hashing is not.
Use Argon2id or scrypt for passwords and a CSPRNG plus hashing for tokens.

misconceptions.description: Encrypting passwords so they can be recovered.
misconceptions.feedback: Password verification never needs the original. A slow salted hash makes a stolen database expensive to attack and avoids a recoverable master key.

misconceptions.description: Believing a random token needs no storage protection.
misconceptions.feedback: Random tokens still leak through database reads and logs. Store only a hash, use a CSPRNG, and expire the token.

misconceptions.description: Treating MD5 with a salt as adequate password storage.
misconceptions.feedback: MD5 is fast by design, which helps an attacker. Use a memory-hard password hash such as Argon2id or scrypt.

sections.title: Three jobs, three tools
sections.body: Password storage needs a slow, salted, one-way hash. Reset and session tokens need unpredictable randomness and hashed storage so a database leak does not hand over live credentials. Encryption is for data you must read again, and it depends on key management.

sections.title: Randomness has grades
sections.body: Math.random is designed for simulations and games, not secrets. Use the platform's cryptographically secure generator. A token that looks long can still be predictable if its source is not a CSPRNG.

sections.title: Transport and storage are separate
sections.body: TLS protects bytes in transit. It does not protect a token stored in plaintext or a password hashed with a fast function. Each layer needs its own control.

vocabulary.definition: A slow, salted, one-way transformation used to verify a password.
Unique random data added before hashing so equal passwords do not collide.
A cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator.
Creating, storing, rotating, and restricting access to encryption keys.
A one-way digest of a bearer token, stored instead of the token itself.

steps.title: Store a password
steps.prompt: The database stores password verifiers. Which operation belongs there?
hints: Verification only needs to compare, not recover.
A fast hash helps an attacker guess quickly.
A unique salt prevents one guess from testing every account.
Choose a slow, salted hash such as Argon2id or scrypt.

quiz.prompt: Which operation should produce the stored password verifier?

options.label: A slow, salted hash such as Argon2id or scrypt
Reversible encryption with a server key

quiz.explanation: Password verification is a one-way comparison. A slow, memory-hard hash with a unique salt raises the cost of offline guessing.

steps.title: Review the reset token flow
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.
hints: Look at how the token is generated.
Check what the database stores and how long it lives.
Ask what a leaked database row would let an attacker do.
Reject the flow: weak randomness, raw storage, and no expiry all need repair.

artifact.title: Password reset token
artifact.caption: The token is emailed, stored, and compared with strict equality.

findings.label: Math.random is not a cryptographically secure token source.
The database stores the live token instead of a hash.
The token has no expiry or single-use condition.
Storing only a hash would limit the damage of a database leak.
A random string never needs to be hashed at rest.

verdicts.label: Reject until generation, storage, and expiry are fixed

steps.explanation: A reset token is a bearer credential. Generate it with a CSPRNG, store a hash, expire it, and consume it once.

steps.title: Match the protection to the threat
hints: Ask whether the system ever needs the original value back.
Separate transit, storage, and key access.
A fast hash is a liability for passwords.
Select slow hashing, hashed tokens, TLS, and key management; reject MD5 and recoverable passwords.

statements.label: Argon2id and scrypt are designed to make password guessing expensive.
A reset token should be stored as a hash so a database leak does not expose it.
TLS protects credentials in transit but not a plaintext token at rest.
Encryption is only as strong as the key management around it.
MD5 with a salt is adequate for password storage.
Passwords should be encrypted so support staff can recover them.

steps.explanation: Use one-way, slow hashing for passwords, CSPRNG tokens stored as hashes, TLS for transit, and explicit key management for reversible encryption.
